Chapter 3

Navigating Chaos

驾驭混乱

You probably didn’t step into this role because everything was going smoothly. Most engineering leaders are hired or promoted because something is broken; a team is behind; trust is shaky; delivery is inconsistent; morale is slipping; the roadmap is on fire—and now it’s yours to fix.

你坐上这个位子，多半不是因为一切都顺风顺水。大多数工程领导者之所以被招进来或被提拔，是因为有什么东西坏了：某个团队落后了、信任动摇了、交付时好时坏、士气在下滑、路线图已经着火——而现在，这一切归你修。

There’s no checklist for this moment, no onboarding guide for chaos. There is just pressure, ambiguity, and a team looking to you for direction.

这种时刻没有清单可照，混乱也没有入职指南。摆在你面前的只有压力、模糊，以及一个眼巴巴指望你给出方向的团队。

Here’s the part that most people won’t admit (or aren’t aware of): you don’t fix this with control; you fix it with range. Figure 3-1 gives you an overview of what this means.

下面这一点，大多数人不肯承认（或者根本没意识到）：你不是靠“控制”来解决问题的，而是靠“幅度（range）”。图 3-1 概览了它的含义。

Range gives you the ability to read the room and adjust. It enables you to lead with clarity when it seems like there is none around you, to be decisive without being rigid, and to calm things down without slowing them down.

幅度，就是你读懂局面、并据此调整的能力。它让你在周围一片混沌时仍能给出清晰的领导，让你果断却不僵化，让你稳住局面却不拖慢节奏。

That’s what this chapter is about. Leadership in chaos isn’t about having the perfect answers; it’s about knowing how to show up effectively and when to shift your stance so the team can move forward, even when everything feels stuck.

这正是本章的主题。混乱中的领导力，不在于你手里有完美答案；而在于你知道如何有效地在场、以及何时切换姿态，好让团队在一切看似僵住时仍能向前走。

We call these shifts switches: deliberate moves in how you lead, tuned to the moment. Rather than being personality changes or performance tricks, they’re adjustments in tone, pace, and focus so that your team gets what they actually need right now.

我们把这种切换叫做“开关（switch）”：根据当下时刻有意调整你的领导方式。它们不是性格改造，也不是表演技巧，而是在语气、节奏和焦点上的调校，好让团队此刻真正得到他们需要的东西。

— 原书第 55 页 —

This chapter walks through the four key switches that make up your leadership range, as identified in Figure 3-1:

本章会逐一讲清构成你领导幅度的四个关键开关，即图 3-1 所示：

  • Diagnose context. Matching your leadership to the moment

    诊断情境。让你的领导方式与当下时刻相匹配。

  • Thrive in chaos. Creating momentum when everything stalls

    在混乱中成长。当一切停摆时，制造前进的势头。

  • Focus on outcomes. Steering attention toward impact, not just activity

    聚焦结果。把注意力引向真正的影响，而不只是忙碌的动作。

  • Shift between roles. Knowing when to be a pilot, medic, or engineer

    在角色间切换。知道何时做领航员、何时做医护、何时下场当工程师。

Each switch is both a lens for reading the situation and a tool for acting with purpose. Together, they give you the range to lead through chaos.

每个开关既是一面用来读懂局面的透镜，也是一件用来有的放矢地行动的工具。它们合在一起，就给了你穿越混乱所需的幅度。

Diagnose Context

诊断情境

Match your leadership to the moment. One of the fastest ways to lose a team is leading them as if they’re somewhere else.

让你的领导方式与当下时刻匹配。失去一个团队最快的方式之一，就是用“他们处在另一个地方”的方式去领导他们。

A startup crew under existential pressure doesn’t need the same guidance as a scaled team optimizing for predictability. A burned-out group struggling through low morale needs a different touch than a hungry team racing toward a deadline. Yet many leaders, especially in chaos, fall back on what worked before. The context has shifted, but their approach hasn’t. That misalignment creates friction, wastes energy, and often makes problems worse instead of better.

一家承受生存压力的初创团队，和一支追求可预测性的扩张期团队，需要的指导并不相同。一群 burnout、士气低落的人，和一支 deadline 前玩命冲刺的饥渴团队，需要的触碰方式也不同。然而许多领导者，尤其是在混乱中，会退回到“过去管用的那一套”。情境已经变了，他们的做法却没变。这种错位制造摩擦、浪费精力，往往让问题越变越糟，而不是变好。

Diagnosing context means understanding the real conditions before you act. When you match your leadership to the moment, your instincts become assets rather than liabilities.

诊断情境，就是在动手之前先理解真实的处境。当你让领导方式与时刻相匹配时，你的直觉会变成资产，而不是负债。

Why Diagnosis Matters More Than Style

为什么诊断比风格更重要

Context isn’t just about structural differences between startups and enterprises, or small teams and large organizations. Effective diagnosis requires reading three distinct dimensions that shape how teams receive and respond to leadership:

情境不只是初创公司与大企业、小团队与大组织之间的结构差异。有效的诊断，需要你读懂三个不同的维度——它们决定了团队如何接收并回应你的领导：

  • Human dimension. This refers to the emotional and psychological state of your people. Are they energized and ready for challenges, or depleted and needing stability? Are trust levels high enough to support risk-taking, or has skepticism created defensive behaviors?

    人的维度。指你团队成员的情绪与心理状态。他们是精力充沛、准备好迎接挑战，还是已经耗竭、急需稳定？信任是否高到足以支撑冒险，还是怀疑已经催生了防御性行为？

  • Operational dimension. This dimension is about the current state of work systems and processes. Are priorities clear and is work visible, or is the team drowning in hidden tasks and competing demands? Is the pace sustainable, or are people constantly putting out fires?

    运营维度。关乎工作系统与流程的当前状态。优先级是否清晰、工作是否可见，还是团队正被隐性任务和互相竞争的需求淹没？节奏是否可持续，还是大家一直在救火？

  • Cultural dimension. The third dimension involves the unspoken rules about what behaviors are rewarded or punished. Does the environment encourage innovation or punish failure? What feels safe versus risky in this particular context?

    文化维度。第三个维度关乎那些不成文的规则：哪些行为会被奖励、哪些会被惩罚。这个环境是鼓励创新，还是惩罚失败？在这个特定情境里，什么让人觉得安全、什么让人觉得冒险？

Each dimension shapes how your team receives and responds to leadership. If you miss any of them, you’ll find yourself pushing solutions that don’t fit the problem.

每个维度都在塑造团队如何接收和回应领导。漏掉任何一个，你都会发现自己在硬塞一些“和问题并不匹配”的解决方案。

— 原书第 57 页 —

Four Lenses for Reading Context

读懂情境的四副透镜

The best way to develop this awareness is by examining the same situation from different lenses. Like the dimensions used to diagnose your context, each lens reveals other aspects of what’s actually happening, helping you choose responses that fit rather than defaulting to familiar patterns that might be entirely wrong for the moment.

培养这种觉察力最好的办法，是透过不同透镜去审视同一个局面。就像用来诊断情境的那几个维度一样，每副透镜都会照出“实际正在发生之事”的另一面，帮你选出合身的应对，而不是退回到那些对当下时刻可能完全错路的熟悉套路。

1. The system lens: What kind of environment are we in?

1. 系统透镜：我们身处什么样的环境？

Every team operates within larger constraints that set the pace, risk tolerance, and types of problems that dominate. If you don’t account for these systemic pressures, you’ll optimize for the wrong things and wonder why nothing works.

每个团队都运行在更大的约束之中——这些约束决定了节奏、风险容忍度，以及占主导地位的问题类型。如果你不把这些系统性压力考虑进去，就会优化错对象，然后纳闷为什么什么都不管用。

A startup team thrives on speed and improvisation, but the same behavior in a compliance-heavy environment creates risks that could kill the company. An enterprise team values predictability and careful coordination, but the same caution in a startup can be equally costly.

初创团队靠速度和即兴发挥茁壮成长；但在一个合规要求极重的环境里，同样的行为会制造足以拖垮公司的风险。企业级团队看重可预测性和谨慎协作；但同样的谨慎放在初创公司里，代价同样高昂。

In startups, hesitation means missing market windows, losing first-mover advantage, and burning runway while competitors move ahead. Customer needs evolve rapidly, and the luxury of extensive planning often doesn’t exist. Teams that spend months perfecting features may discover the market has shifted, funding has dried up, or a competitor has captured the opportunity. The cost of moving slowly can literally be business survival. Startups typically have limited time and resources to find product–market fit before running out of capital.

在初创公司里，犹豫就意味着错过市场窗口、丧失先发优势，并在对手向前跑的时候烧掉自己的跑道。客户需求变化极快，往往根本没有“从容做大量规划”这种奢侈。花上几个月打磨功能的团队，可能最后发现市场已经变了、融资断了，或者机会早已被对手抢走。动作慢的代价， literally 就是公司的生死。初创公司在烧光钱之前，通常只有有限的时间和资源去找到产品与市场的匹配（product–market fit）。

Enterprise caution that works in established markets becomes a liability when speed determines whether you capture emerging opportunities or lose them forever. In Table 3-1 we summarize how different organizational stages require different strategies for success.

在成熟市场里行之有效的企业式谨慎，一旦遇到“速度决定你能否抓住新兴机会、还是永远失去它”的局面，就会变成负债。表 3-1 总结了不同组织阶段为何需要不同的成功策略。

2. The human lens: What shape are my people in?

2. 人的透镜：我的团队成员状态如何？

The same system can feel completely different depending on your team’s emotional and mental state. Morale, trust, and energy levels determine whether people can absorb new challenges or need stability first. Table 3-2 highlights some of the warning signs and suggested responses for concerns in these categories.

同一个系统，在团队不同的情绪与精神状态下，感受会截然不同。士气、信任和精力水平，决定了人们是能承接新挑战，还是需要先稳住阵脚。表 3-2 列出了这几类问题的一些预警信号与建议应对。

Here’s the thing about burnout: it often masquerades as resistance. A team that seems disengaged might actually be exhausted from months of navigating chaos or organizational churn. Pushing harder in these moments deepens the problem rather than solving it. Therefore, it’s important for leaders to distinguish between genuine resistance and capacity depletion before choosing their response.

关于 burnout，有一点很关键：它常常伪装成抵触。一个看起来心不在焉的团队，可能实际上是在数月的混乱或组织动荡中被耗干了。这种时候再加大推力，只会让问题更深，而不是解决它。因此，领导者在选择应对方式之前，必须先分清“真正的抵触”和“承载力耗尽”。

Resistance shows up as active pushbacks and vocal concerns. Burnout masquerades as withdrawal, declining quality, and hollow compliance. People stop volunteering ideas and just go through the motions.

抵触表现为主动的反对和大声的担忧；burnout 则伪装成退缩、质量下滑和敷衍式服从。人们不再主动出主意，只是走个过场。

The interventions are opposite: resistance needs vision clarification and buy-in rebuilding; burnout needs capacity protection—slowing down, reducing scope, or creating recovery time before pushing forward.

两者的干预方式恰恰相反：抵触需要澄清愿景、重建认同；burnout 需要保护承载力——放慢节奏、缩小范围，或者在硬推之前先留出恢复时间。

You can have perfect strategy and culture, but if your people are running on empty, everything will feel like resistance. Sometimes leaders need to step back to move forward more effectively.

你可以有完美的战略和文化，但如果你的人已经跑空了油，一切都会被感受成抵触。有时候，领导者需要先后退一步，才能更有效地向前。

3. The work lens: What’s actually on the plate?

3. 工作透镜：盘子里到底装了什么？

Teams can appear dysfunctional when the real issue is invisible or misaligned work. Even high-performing groups struggle under hidden support requests, unclear priorities, or a difficult ratio of unplanned to planned work. Table 3-3 outlines some of these productivity illusions and possible solutions.

当真正的问题是隐性工作或错配工作时，团队看起来会像功能失调。即便是高绩效团队，在隐性的支持请求、不清的优先级，或者计划外与计划内工作糟糕的比例下，也会举步维艰。表 3-3 列出了一些“生产率幻觉”及可能的解法。

4. 文化透镜：那些不成文的规则是什么？

The Reality of Power and Identity

权力与身份的现实

Here’s what most leadership advice doesn’t tell you: context diagnosis isn’t neutral. Your background, identity, and position within the organization influence what you can see and the actions available to you. You’ve probably felt it, but you have to lean into it.

大多数领导建议不会告诉你这一点：情境诊断并不是中立的。你的背景、身份、以及你在组织中的位置，都会影响你能看见什么、以及你手上有哪些可用的动作。你大概早已感觉到了，但你必须坦然面对它。

Some leaders can challenge executives directly and walk away with increased trust. Others face higher scrutiny for the same behavior due to their background, accent, or visible identity markers. Leaders from underrepresented backgrounds frequently navigate additional political complexity that affects which leadership approaches are viable, and those holding multiple marginalized identities may face compounded challenges that shift based on context.

有些领导者可以当面挑战高管，事后反而赢得更多信任；另一些人仅仅因为背景、口音或可见的身份标识，做同样的事就要面对更苛刻的审视。来自代表性不足背景的领导者，常常要额外应对一层政治复杂性——这会决定哪些领导方式可行；而同时背负多重边缘化身份的人，可能面临层层叠加、且随情境变化的挑战。

While this may not be fair, understanding your constraints will help you to choose strategies that work within your actual sphere of influence rather than an idealized version that exists only in leadership books that don’t consider these factors.

尽管这不公平，但认清自己的约束，会帮你选出在“你真实的影响范围”内管用的策略，而不是照本宣科地套用那些根本不考虑这些因素的领导力书里的理想化版本。

— 原书第 60 页 —

We’re not writing this from a neutral position either. As coauthors—both bald, tattooed men, one Colombian, one Australian—we’ve learned that while we may share the baldness, our boldness shows up in different ways. Accents get noticed and assumptions are made. Through this, we’ve learned that the leadership approaches that work for one of us might not work for the other.

我们写这些，也并非站在一个中立的位置上。作为共同作者——两个都光头、都有纹身的男人，一个哥伦比亚人、一个澳大利亚人——我们体会到：虽然我们共享了光头，但我们的“大胆”是以不同方式呈现的。口音会被注意到，别人也会据此做各种假设。由此我们学到，对我们其中一人管用的领导方式，对另一个人未必管用。

It is important to keep this in mind when anyone gives you leadership advice—including us. What works in our contexts might completely miss the mark in yours. Because frameworks can be adapted, they matter more than specific tactics, which might land you in trouble if they don’t match your reality.

所以，当任何人（包括我们）给你领导建议时，都要把这一点记在心里。在我们的情境里管用的东西，放到你的情境里可能完全不着调。框架是可以改造的，因此框架比具体战术更重要——因为战术一旦和你的现实不匹配，就可能让你惹上麻烦。

A senior engineer might need to build coalition support before proposing process changes, while a director could simply mandate them. A new manager from an underrepresented background might need to establish credibility differently than someone whose authority is automatically assumed.

一个高级工程师可能需要先建立联盟支持，再提议改变流程；而一位总监则可以直接下令推行。来自代表性不足背景的新任经理，建立公信力的方式，可能必须与那种“权威被默认”的人不同。

The goal isn’t about accepting limitations, but rather about working with reality. Sometimes the most effective approach is indirect: finding allies, demonstrating results at a small scale, or reframing proposals to align with existing organizational priorities. Sometimes it’s a direct challenge. The skill is knowing which approach fits your context, not ours.

目标不是接受局限，而是与现实共事。有时候最有效的方式是间接的：找到盟友、在小范围做出结果，或者重新包装提案使其对齐组织现有的优先级。有时候则需要直接挑战。真正的本事，是知道哪种方式契合你的情境——而不是我们的情境。

Rapid Assessment When You’re New

刚入职时的快速评估

When you’re new to an organization, you lack the historical context that makes diagnosis easier. You can’t distinguish between temporary stress and chronic dysfunction, or between individual quirks and systemic patterns.

刚进入一个组织时，你缺少那份让诊断变得容易的历史背景。你分不清什么是暂时的压力、什么是长期的功能失调；也分不清什么是个人怪癖、什么是系统性模式。

Start with observation before action. For example, attend meetings without immediately trying to fix them, read Slack channels to understand communication patterns, or follow a deploy or incident response to see how the team actually operates under pressure.

先观察，再行动。比如：去开会，但别急着一上来就想修好它；读 Slack 频道，去理解沟通模式；或者跟着一次部署或事故响应，看看团队在压力下到底是怎么运转的。

Ask diagnostic questions like the following, which will help you to understand the dynamics rather than just facts:

多问一些下面这类诊断性问题——它们帮你理解的是动态关系，而不只是事实：

  • What’s working well that I should be careful not to break?

    哪些事情运转得很好，我必须小心别去破坏它？

  • What keeps falling through the cracks despite good intentions?

    明明大家好意满满，却总是掉进缝隙的是什么？

  • Where does the team feel most confident about our current approach, and where do they feel the least confident?

    团队对现在的做法，哪里最有信心，哪里最没底？

Find multiple perspectives. Quiet team members often have different insights than vocal ones. Similarly, individual conversations reveal information that never surfaces in group settings. Look for patterns across conversations rather than taking any single viewpoint as the complete truth.

去找多种视角。安静的成员往往和话多的人有不同的洞见。同样，一对一谈话会暴露那些在群体场合里永远浮不出水面的信息。要在多场谈话之间寻找规律，而不是把任何单一观点当成全部真相。

— 原书第 61 页 —

In addition, it can be helpful to test small hypotheses. Rather than making significant changes based on incomplete information, run small experiments that reveal how the system responds. Propose a minor process adjustment and observe the resistance or support that emerges.

此外，去检验一些小假设也很有帮助。不要在信息不完整时做大改动，而是做一些小实验，让系统的反应自己暴露出来。比如提议一个小小的流程调整，然后观察会冒出怎样的抵触或支持。

When Diagnosis Reveals Hard Truths

当诊断揭示出残酷真相时

Sometimes, context assessment reveals that the real problems lie beyond your level or outside your control. The team isn’t dysfunctional; they’re responding rationally to irrational constraints. The underlying issues aren’t just about code quality; they stem from years of business pressure to deliver quickly rather than invest in long-term stability.

有时候，情境评估会揭示：真正的问题在你的层级之上、或在你的控制之外。团队并不是功能失调——他们只是在对不合理的约束做出理性反应。深层问题也不只是代码质量，而是源于多年来“快速交付、不愿投资长期稳定”的业务压力。

In these situations, naming the context becomes crucial. You can’t solve every systemic problem, but you can help your team understand what they’re navigating and make informed choices about where to invest energy.

在这种情况下，把情境“说破”就变得至关重要。你解决不了每一个系统性问题，但你可以帮团队看清自己正在穿越什么，并就“把精力投到哪里”做出知情的选择。

A team struggling with constant interruptions might need better boundaries, but they also need leadership acknowledgment that the current system creates unsustainable demands. Similarly, a group frustrated by slow decision making might benefit from clearer escalation paths, but they also need recognition that the broader organization rewards consensus over speed.

一个被无休止打断折磨的团队，可能需要更好的边界，但他们同样需要领导者承认：是当前这套系统在制造不可持续的要求。同样，一个被缓慢决策折磨的团队，可能受益于更清晰的升级路径，但他们也需要被看见：整个更大的组织奖励的是共识，而不是速度。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April stared at the incident report from last night’s outage: 30 minutes of downtime, angry customers, and her team scrambling to fix a deployment that should have been routine. The system lens revealed to her that they were in chaos during scale-up, with growth outpacing their deployment infrastructure. The human lens revealed her team was exhausted from six months of firefighting. The work lens revealed a previously hidden operational burden that was consuming 40% of their capacity. The cultural lens revealed that PixelCurl prioritized fast shipping over safe shipping.

April 盯着昨夜事故的报告：30 分钟宕机、愤怒的客户，以及她的团队手忙脚乱地抢修一次本该很常规的部署。系统透镜让她看清：他们正处在扩张期的混乱里，增长跑赢了部署基础设施。人的透镜让她看清：团队已经连续救火六个月、精疲力竭。工作透镜让她看清：有一份此前被隐藏的运营负担，吃掉了他们 40% 的产能。文化透镜则让她看清：PixelCurl 把“快速上线”排在了“安全上线”前面。

Every lens pointed to the same conclusion: this wasn’t a technical problem that needed a technical solution. It was a systemic mismatch between their infrastructure maturity and business velocity expectations. April realized she’d been trying to solve an organizational problem with better monitoring tools when what she really needed was to shift how leadership thought about platform investment versus feature speed.

四副透镜指向同一个结论：这不是一个需要技术方案来解决的技术问题，而是基础设施成熟度与业务速度期望之间的系统性错配。April 意识到，自己一直在用“更好的监控工具”去解决一个组织问题，而她真正需要的，是转变领导层对“平台投资 vs. 功能速度”的看法。

Connecting Diagnosis to Action

把诊断连接到行动

Context diagnosis only matters if it changes what you do. Each of the following insight lenses should inform specific leadership adjustments rather than just giving you more things to think about:

情境诊断只有在它改变了你的行动时才有意义。下面每一副洞察透镜，都应当转化为具体的领导调整，而不只是给你增添更多“要想的事”：

— 原书第 62 页 —

  • System insights guide your pace and communication style. In high-pressure environments, shorter cycles and more frequent check-ins might be necessary. In stable environments, you have more time for consultation and building consensus.

    系统洞察指导你的节奏与沟通方式。在高压环境里，可能需要更短的周期和更频繁的对齐；在稳定环境里，你才有更多时间去商议、去建立共识。

  • Human insights shape your emotional approach. Exhausted teams need encouragement and protection. Anxious teams need clarity and predictability. Confident teams can handle more ambiguity and challenge.

    人的洞察塑造你的情绪应对。耗竭的团队需要鼓励和保护；焦虑的团队需要清晰和可预测；自信的团队则能承受更多模糊与挑战。

  • Work insights drive operational changes. Hidden work needs visibility tools. Misaligned work needs priority clarification. Unsustainable work needs capacity protection.

    工作洞察驱动运营层面的改变。隐性工作需要可视化工具；错配的工作需要澄清优先级；不可持续的工作需要保护产能。

  • Cultural insights inform your political strategy. Some environments reward direct challenge, while others require careful coalition building. Additionally, some environments prize individual heroics, while others value collaborative achievement.

    文化洞察决定你的政治策略。有些环境奖励直接挑战，另一些则需要你小心翼翼地建立联盟；有些环境推崇个人英雄主义，另一些则看重协作式的成就。

The goal isn’t a perfect diagnosis; it’s a good enough assessment to avoid significant mismatches between what you do and what the situation requires.

目标不是做出完美诊断，而是做出“足够好”的评估，避免你的行动与情境要求之间出现重大错配。

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April made this discovery when she realized her team’s lack of strategy alignment was a major problem. The system pressures (scale-up chaos), human factors (uneven morale and trust), work patterns (hidden operational tasks), and cultural dynamics (speed rewarded over stability) all required coordinated responses. Her breakthrough came from addressing multiple dimensions simultaneously rather than treating each as a separate problem.

April 是在意识到“团队缺乏战略对齐”本身就是个大问题时，得到这个发现的。系统压力（扩张期混乱）、人的因素（士气与信任不均）、工作模式（隐性运营任务）、文化动态（奖励速度而非稳定），全都需要协同应对。她的突破在于：同时处理多个维度，而不是把每个维度当成孤立问题来解决。

Context diagnosis is a skill that improves with practice. The more situations you navigate, the faster you can recognize patterns and adjust accordingly. But it starts with the discipline to pause and assess before you act, even when the pressure to do something—anything—feels overwhelming.

情境诊断是一项靠练习精进的技能。你穿越的局面越多，就越快能识别模式并据此调整。但它始于一种纪律：在行动之前先停下来评估——哪怕那种“得做点什么、随便做点什么”的压力让你喘不过气。

Thrive in Chaos

在混乱中成长

When things fall apart, most leaders grab for control. They often think they need to add approval layers or implement more checkpoints. But what results is an environment where everyone feels busy but achieves nothing. The instinct makes sense because chaos feels scary and control feels safe. But what we’ve learned, after watching teams implode and rebuild, is that control is often the problem, not the solution.

当事情崩塌时，大多数领导者会本能地去抓“控制”。他们常常觉得需要加审批层级、设更多检查点。但结果却是：人人都觉得很忙，却一事无成。这种本能可以理解——因为混乱让人害怕，而控制让人安全。但在看过一个个团队内爆又重建之后，我们学到的是：控制往往本身就是问题，而不是解法。

— 原书第 63 页 —

It’s the management equivalent of putting duct tape on a cracked foundation. It might hold for a week, but the house is still falling.

这在管理上，相当于在开裂的地基上贴胶带。它也许能撑一周，但房子依然在塌。

The Trap of Bureaucratic Control

官僚式控制的陷阱

Bureaucratic, or hierarchical, control seems attractive when your team is drowning. If deadlines are slipping, trust is shot, and nobody knows what anybody else is doing, it’s easy to feel out of control. Leaping to introduce structures is a method that many leaders follow because they think it will make them feel more in control.

当你的团队溺水时，官僚式（或层级式）控制看起来很诱人。deadline 一拖再拖、信任已经崩掉、没人知道别人在干什么——这种时候，人很容易觉得“失控”。于是许多领导者一把扑上去搞流程架构，因为他们以为那样会让自己重新感到“一切尽在掌握”。

So, what do most leaders do? They call more meetings, add more sign-offs, and create more reports that nobody reads but which everyone is still required to write. Now your team is drowning and filling out paperwork.

那么大多数领导者做了什么？他们开更多的会、加更多的签核、做更多没人读但人人都得写的报告。结果你的团队一边溺水，一边还在填表格。

This isn’t about being anti-process. Smart teams need good architectural decisions, incident protocols, and clear ownership when things break. But there’s a difference between infrastructure that helps people do their job and bureaucracy that becomes the job.

这并不是说要反对流程。聪明的团队需要好的架构决策、事故处理规程，以及出问题时清晰的责任归属。但“帮人们把活干成的基础设施”和“本身变成了工作的官僚主义”，是两回事。

Bureaucratic control feels productive because it creates visible activity—meetings are scheduled, documents are reviewed, and approvals are tracked. But none of that creates forward momentum. When teams are already struggling with broken trust or unclear priorities, adding process overhead deepens the dysfunction rather than solving it.

官僚式控制感觉很有产出，因为它制造了可见的动作——会议排上了、文档审过了、审批在追踪了。但这些都不会产生向前的势头。当团队本就困在破碎的信任或不清的优先级里时，再加流程 overhead，只会加深功能失调，而不是解决它。

The Punk Alternative: Motion Creates Clarity

朋克式替代：动起来，才会清晰

Punk understood this distinction in the 1970s. When the music industry became bloated with gatekeepers and elaborate approval processes, punk didn’t try to reform the system; it bypassed it entirely.

朋克在 1970 年代就懂了这个区别。当音乐工业被各种“守门人”和繁琐审批流程塞得臃肿时，朋克没有去改革这套体系——它干脆整个绕了过去。

Record executives in suits were deciding what people wanted to hear and creating elaborate processes for everything. Want to make music? Get in line behind the gatekeepers.

穿着西装的唱片公司高管在决定人们想听什么，并为每件事都设计出繁琐流程。想做音乐？先在守门人后面排队吧。

But punk said, “Forget that approach entirely.”

但朋克说：“那一套，整个忘掉。”

The Ramones, for example, recorded their debut album in seven days. Most bands today spend longer than that picking snare sounds. Minor Threat put out eight songs in under 10 minutes and called it an album. Black Flag lived in a van and played anywhere that would have them—basements, community centers, somebody’s garage.

比如 Ramones，他们用七天录完了首张专辑。今天大多数乐队光是挑军鼓音色就要花更久。Minor Threat 在不到十分钟里塞了八首歌，还管它叫一张专辑。Black Flag 住在一辆面包车里，任何愿意接他们的地方都演——地下室、社区中心、谁家的车库。

Here’s what they understood: motion creates clarity. You don’t get good by planning to get good; you get good by doing the thing, failing fast, and doing it again better. The Ramones didn’t wait for the perfect studio or the right producer; they just plugged in and played.

他们悟到的是：动起来，才会清晰。你不是靠“计划变好”而变好的；你是靠真的去做、快速失败、然后做得更好一点，才变好的。Ramones 没有等完美的录音室或合适的制作人；他们直接插上电就开演。

— 原书第 64 页 —

As Gorilla Biscuits said, “Let’s start today.”

正如 Gorilla Biscuits 所唱：“咱们今天就开始。”

That energy—that bias toward action—is what gets teams unstuck when everything else has failed. However, energy alone isn’t enough.

那股能量——那种“偏向行动”的本能——正是当其他一切都失败时，把团队从僵局里拽出来的东西。然而，光有能量还不够。

From Energy to Discipline

从能量到纪律

Some punk scenes burned out fast—all energy, no structure. People got exhausted, and the movement collapsed.

有些朋克圈子烧得很快——全是能量，没有结构。人们精疲力竭，这场运动也就垮了。

But hardcore punk learned from those mistakes. They adopted the same speed and urgency, but with something punk didn’t always have: discipline and sustainable practices.

但硬核朋克（hardcore punk）从这些错误里学到了教训。他们保留了同样的速度和紧迫感，但加上了朋克并不总有的东西：纪律和可持续的做法。

Hardcore bands shared vans and gear. They created zines to keep scenes connected across cities, building networks that lasted because they weren’t just about individual expression; they were about community. Minor Threat’s “Straight Edge” was more than just a song about not drinking—it was a commitment to showing up clearheaded and focused, to building something that mattered.

硬核乐队合用面包车和设备。他们办自制小报（zines），让不同城市的圈子保持连接，建起持久的网络——因为他们关心的不只是个人表达，更是共同体。Minor Threat 的《Straight Edge》不只是一首讲“不喝酒”的歌，它是一个承诺：清醒而专注地到场，去建设某种真正重要的东西。

That’s the evolution every leader needs to make—from creating motion to creating sustainable motion, from moving fast to moving fast together. The music was urgent, but the community was built to last.

这正是每个领导者都需要完成的进化：从“制造动作”到“制造可持续的动作”，从“一个人跑得快”到“一起跑得快”。音乐是紧迫的，但共同体是为持久而建的。

Open Source: Punk Principles at Scale

开源：规模化的朋克原则

The same ethos that drove hardcore scenes shaped early computing culture, though nobody called it punk leadership at the time.

驱动硬核圈子的那套精神，也塑造了早期的计算文化——尽管当时没人把它叫做“朋克式领导力”。

When something broke, you fixed it yourself. When you needed a tool that didn’t exist, you built it. When you figured something out, you shared it so the next person didn’t have to start from scratch. It was a deliberate approach to solving problems without waiting for permission.

东西坏了，你自己修；需要一个不存在的工具，你自己造；你搞明白了一件事，就分享出去，好让下一个人不必从零开始。这是一种刻意的做事方式：不等许可，直接解决问题。

Linux wasn’t built by committees. PostgreSQL wasn’t designed by focus groups. Apache didn’t come from a corporate roadmap. They came from people who saw problems and solved them, who shared code because making everyone else’s life easier made their own life easier too.

Linux 不是委员会造出来的，PostgreSQL 不是焦点小组设计出来的，Apache 也不是出自某张企业路线图。它们出自这样一群人：看见了问题就动手解决，愿意共享代码——因为让别人的日子好过，自己的日子也好过。

Leadership in these communities came from contribution, not titles. Influence was earned commit by commit. Coordination replaced control, and shared values replaced rigid hierarchy.

在这些共同体里，领导力来自贡献，而不是头衔。影响力是一个 commit 一个 commit 挣来的。协调取代了控制，共享价值观取代了僵化的等级。

However, open source also reveals the limitations of purely do-it-yourself approaches. Projects struggle with maintainer burnout, governance gets messy when egos collide, and funding models break down. The lesson isn’t that these principles are perfect; it’s that they’re powerful when you apply them thoughtfully.

然而，开源也暴露了纯“自己动手”路线的局限：项目会被维护者 burnout 折磨，自我膨胀相撞时治理会一塌糊涂，资助模式也会崩解。教训不是这些原则完美无缺，而是：当你审慎地运用它们时，它们很有力量。

— 原书第 65 页 —

What This Means for Seasoned Leaders

这对资深领导者意味着什么

You’re not starting a band or maintaining a GitHub repository. You’re leading engineering teams with real deadlines, actual stakeholders, and quarterly objectives that matter. But the principles still apply, especially when standard approaches aren’t working.

你不是在组一支乐队，也不是在维护一个 GitHub 仓库。你领导的工程团队有真实的 deadline、真实的利益相关方、以及真正重要的季度目标。但这些原则依然成立——尤其是当标准做法不管用的时候。

When your roadmap doesn’t survive contact with reality, don’t add more planning meetings. Rather, ship something small and learn from it. When executives are stuck debating strategy, prototype the most likely path and give them something concrete to react to. When everyone knows a process is broken but nobody wants to own fixing it, write the first draft yourself. These aren’t heroic gestures. They’re practical moves that restore momentum when teams get stuck in analysis paralysis or bureaucratic quicksand.

当你的路线图一撞上现实就碎掉时，别再加更多规划会。相反，先发一个小东西，从中学习。当高管们困在战略辩论里出不来时，把最有可能的那条路做个原型，给他们一个具体的东西去反应。当人人都知道某个流程坏了、却没人愿意认领修它时，自己先写第一版草稿。这些都不是英雄式姿态，而是实用动作——当团队困在“分析瘫痪”或“官僚流沙”里时，靠它们恢复势头。

The key is reading the situation correctly. Some teams need more structure, not less. Some environments punish anyone who circumvents established channels. Moving fast in a compliance-heavy industry can create legal problems that make your speed irrelevant.

关键在于把局面读对。有些团队需要的是更多结构，而不是更少；有些环境会惩罚任何绕开既定渠道的人。在一个合规要求极重的行业里图快，可能制造出法律问题，让你的速度变得毫无意义。

The most effective framework is to distinguish between constraints that serve the work and constraints that serve themselves. Then act accordingly.

最有效的框架，是分清“为工作服务的约束”和“为约束自身服务的约束”，然后据此行动。

The Political Reality

政治现实

Leading like this inside corporate environments comes with career risk, and that’s something that experienced leaders need to acknowledge honestly.

在企业环境里这样领导，是要承担职业风险的——资深领导者必须诚实地承认这一点。

Some organizations love unorthodox leaders who get things done, while others punish anyone who colors outside the lines. As a staff engineer or middle manager, you might see exactly what needs fixing but lack the political capital to fix it. This is where the hardcore lesson becomes crucial: sustainable change requires community, not just individual action. Sometimes the right move is starting small, demonstrating results, and letting success create permission for bigger changes. Sometimes it’s finding allies who can support you while you experiment with new approaches.

有的组织喜欢能把事做成、不按常理出牌的领导者；另一些组织则会惩罚任何“出格”的人。作为 staff 工程师或中层经理，你可能一眼就看出该修什么，却没有足够的政治资本去修。这时硬核的教训就变得关键：可持续的改变需要共同体，而不只是个人行动。有时候正确的做法是从小处开始、做出结果，让成功为更大的改变创造许可；有时候则是找到盟友，在你试验新做法时为你兜底。

Build the coalition before you build the solution. The goal is to distinguish between constraints that serve the work and constraints that serve the constraint.

在搭建方案之前，先搭建联盟。目标仍然是分清：哪些约束是为工作服务的，哪些约束只是为约束自身服务的。

When Momentum Matters Most

势头最关键的时刻

Punk leadership shows up in specific moments that experienced leaders recognize: when circular debates need decisive action, when teams feel stuck due to unclear priorities, when broken processes consume more energy than they create.

朋克式领导会在某些特定时刻登场——资深领导者一眼就能认出来：当循环往复的辩论需要一个果断动作时；当团队因优先级不清而感到僵住时；当坏掉的流程消耗的能量比它创造的还多时。

In these situations, the worst move isn’t making the wrong decision; it’s not deciding at all.

在这种局面里，最糟的动作不是做了错误决定，而是根本不做决定。

— 原书第 66 页 —

Progress is possible even when conditions aren’t perfect. Sometimes the best way forward is the simplest: stop waiting for permission and start fixing what’s broken. As Youth of Today put it, “It’s time to make a change.” In chaos, trying with intention and discipline beats having the perfect plan every time.

即便条件不完美，进展依然可能发生。有时候最好的前进方式就是最简单的：别再等许可，开始去修那些坏掉的东西。正如 Youth of Today 所唱：“是时候做出改变了。”在混乱中，带着意图和纪律去试，每一次都胜过手握完美计划。

Focus on Outcomes

聚焦结果

In unstable environments, teams grab onto what they can measure, such as sprint velocity, story points, and deployment frequency. The standups are full, the roadmap is moving, and code gets shipped. From a distance, everything looks productive. But when you ask, “What exactly did we achieve?” the answers become vague.

在不稳定的环境里，团队会死死抓住那些能度量的东西：sprint 速度、故事点、部署频率。站会开得满满当当，路线图在往前推，代码也在上线。远远看去，一切都很有产出。但当你问“我们到底取得了什么成果？”时，答案就变得含糊。

This isn’t laziness or lack of focus; it’s a survival response. When everything feels uncertain, measurable activity provides psychological safety. But activity without direction burns people out faster than honest idleness. Don’t confuse activity with progress. Your job as a leader is to cut through the motion and point toward impact that actually matters.

这不是懒惰，也不是不专注；这是一种生存反应。当一切都不确定时，可度量的活动能提供心理安全感。但没有方向的忙碌，比坦诚的闲置更快地把人烧干。别把活动当成进展。作为领导者，你的工作就是穿透这些动作，指向真正重要的影响。

The Sophistication Trap

“高级感”陷阱

Experienced teams fall into activity traps differently than novice ones. They don’t track meaningless vanity metrics or celebrate meaningless milestones. Instead, they prioritize work that seems sophisticated and feels important, even if it disconnects from business reality: architecture discussions that never conclude, refactoring sprints that improve code quality but don’t unlock new capabilities, elaborate planning processes that consume more time than the work they organize, and process improvements that make work feel more organized without making it more effective.

有经验的团队掉进“活动陷阱”的方式，和新手团队不同。他们不会去追踪毫无意义的虚荣指标，也不会庆祝毫无意义的里程碑。相反，他们会优先做那些看起来高深、感觉重要的事——哪怕它和业务现实已经脱钩：永远开不出结论的架构讨论、提升了代码质量却没有解锁任何新能力的重构 sprint、比它所组织的工作本身还要耗时的繁琐规划流程、以及那些让工作“看起来更有条理”却并未更有效的流程改进。

While none of this is wasteful in isolation, these activities become traps when they turn into ends in themselves rather than means to customer or business outcomes. Teams can spend months perfecting systems that don’t solve problems anyone actually has.

单看每一件都不算浪费；但当这些活动从“达成客户或业务结果的手段”变成“目的本身”时，它们就成了陷阱。团队可能花上好几个月去打磨一套系统，而这套系统解决的问题，其实根本没人真有。

Why Outcome Frameworks Miss the Point

为什么结果框架常常不得要领

Most outcome frameworks, such as objectives and key results (OKRs), fail because they address symptoms rather than causes. Teams write better objectives, track cleaner metrics, and still drift toward irrelevance. The problem isn’t the measurement technique; it’s the assumption that clarity comes from better goal setting rather than better context understanding.

大多数结果框架（比如 OKR）之所以失败，是因为它们治标不治本。团队写出更好的目标、追踪更干净的指标，却依然滑向无关紧要。问题不在度量技术本身，而在那个假设：以为清晰来自“更好地设定目标”，而不是“更好地理解情境”。

Outcome focus isn’t about writing perfect OKRs or creating elaborate dashboards anymore. It’s about building the organizational muscle to separate meaningful progress from mere activity, to recognize when work matters and when it doesn’t, and to make trade-offs based on impact rather than ease or familiarity.

聚焦结果，早已不是写出完美 OKR、做华丽仪表盘那么简单。它是要在组织里练出一块肌肉：把“有意义的进展”和“单纯的活动”区分开；分辨什么时候工作重要、什么时候不重要；并基于影响而非“顺手”或“熟悉”来做取舍。

— 原书第 67 页 —

This requires different approaches in different contexts. A startup team needs to iterate quickly toward product–market fit, accepting that many experiments will fail. An enterprise platform team needs to make infrastructure investments that might not show business impact for quarters. A team inheriting legacy technical debt needs to balance maintenance with feature development.

这在不同情境下需要不同做法。初创团队需要快速迭代、逼近产品市场匹配，并接受许多实验会失败；企业平台团队需要做那些可能几个季度都看不到业务影响的基础设施投资；接手历史技术债的团队，则需要在维护和功能开发之间取得平衡。

The framework isn’t the same metrics for everyone, but it is the same discipline—connecting daily work to meaningful outcomes, even when those connections are indirect or delayed.

这个框架不是给所有人同一组指标，但它是同一种纪律——把日常工作连回有意义的结果，哪怕这种连接是间接的、或滞后的。

When Outcomes Are Genuinely Unclear

当结果真的说不清时

Real leadership situations don’t come with predefined success criteria. You’re often working through genuine uncertainty about what outcomes to pursue, let alone how to measure them.

真实的领导局面，并不会附一份预先定义好的成功标准。你常常是在真正的不确定中摸索——连“该追求什么结果”都不清楚，更别说怎么度量它了。

Exploratory product work doesn’t have predetermined outcomes. You’re iterating toward understanding, not executing against a known goal. Success might mean discovering that an approach doesn’t work, which prevents months of wasted effort.

探索性的产品工作没有预先设定的结果。你是在朝“理解”迭代，而不是对着一个已知目标执行。成功可能意味着：发现某条路走不通——从而避免了好几个月的白费力气。

Technical architecture decisions have indirect business impact. The outcome might be enabling future development speed or reducing operational risk, neither of which shows up in quarterly metrics. You’re building capabilities that enable other people to create value.

技术架构决策的业务影响是间接的。结果可能是让未来开发更快、或降低运营风险——这两者都不会出现在季度指标里。你是在搭建能力，让别人能借此创造价值。

Platform and infrastructure investments create value through what they enable rather than what they directly produce. The outcome is often invisible to end users but crucial for engineering productivity. You’re optimizing for leverage, not immediate output.

平台与基础设施投资创造价值的方式，是通过它们“赋能了什么”，而不是它们“直接产出了什么”。这种结果对终端用户往往不可见，但对工程生产率至关重要。你优化的是杠杆，而不是即时产出。

In these situations, outcome focus means being explicit about the hypothesis you’re testing or the capability you’re building, even when the business impact is uncertain or delayed. The goal is to arrive at an honest acknowledgment of what you’re trying to achieve and why it matters.

在这种局面下，聚焦结果意味着：哪怕业务影响尚不确定或滞后，你也要把“你正在检验的假设”或“你正在搭建的能力”讲清楚。目标是诚实地承认：你到底想达成什么、以及它为什么重要。

The Political Dimension

政治维度

Outcome clarity becomes complicated when your team’s success conflicts with other stakeholders’ incentives. Your engineering team might optimize for system reliability while the business team optimizes for feature velocity. Your infrastructure improvements might slow down feature delivery in the short term. Rather than being technical problems to solve with better metrics, they’re political realities to navigate with more transparent communication and stronger alliances.

当你团队的成功与其他利益相关方的激励相冲突时，结果清晰就变得复杂起来。你的工程团队可能在优化系统可靠性，而业务团队在优化功能交付速度；你的基础设施改进，短期内可能拖慢功能交付。这些不是“用更好的指标就能解决”的技术问题，而是需要用更透明的沟通和更牢固的联盟去应对的政治现实。

Sometimes the right move is reframing your outcomes in language that aligns with broader organizational priorities. Technical debt reduction becomes “increasing feature delivery predictability.” Infrastructure investment becomes “reducing business risk from outages.” You’re translating engineering value into business language.

有时候正确的做法，是用与组织更大优先级对齐的语言重新包装你的结果。“偿还技术债”变成“提升功能交付的可预测性”；“基础设施投资”变成“降低宕机带来的业务风险”。你是在把工程价值翻译成业务语言。

— 原书第 68 页 —

Sometimes you need to surface the tension and help leadership make informed trade-offs explicitly. For example, you could say, “We can ship faster by accumulating technical debt, or invest in stability and move more deliberately. Both have costs.” The sophistication is knowing when to align, when to push back, and when to document disagreement while moving forward.

有时候你需要把这种张力摆上台面，帮领导层做出明确、知情的取舍。比如你可以说：“我们可以靠积累技术债来发得更快，也可以投资稳定性、走得更稳。两者都有代价。”真正的老练，是知道何时对齐、何时顶回去、以及何时在继续前进的同时把异议记录在案。

Context Shapes Outcome Focus

情境塑造结果聚焦

Your approach to outcomes depends heavily on your diagnostic assessment. The same outcome might require completely different approaches based on your team’s situation. Let’s consider the four contexts we’ve been discussing.

你对待结果的方式，很大程度上取决于你的诊断评估。同一个结果，根据团队处境不同，可能需要完全不同的打法。我们来回顾前面一直在讨论的四种情境。

System context determines your time horizon. Startup environments might measure outcomes in weeks. Enterprise environments, on the other hand, plan for quarters or years. Platform teams might work toward capabilities that won’t show impact until other teams build on them.

系统情境决定你的时间跨度。初创环境可能以周为单位度量结果；企业环境则以季度或年度做规划。平台团队可能在打造一种能力——要等其他团队在它之上建东西，它的影响才会显现。

The human context will affect how you communicate outcomes. Burned-out teams need to see progress quickly to rebuild confidence, while energized teams can sustain longer feedback loops if they understand the strategic rationale. Teams with low trust need smaller, more frequent wins.

人的情境会影响你如何沟通结果。被 burnout 的团队需要快速看到进展来重建信心；而精力充沛的团队，如果理解背后的战略理由，可以承受更长的反馈回路。信任度低的团队，则需要更小、更频繁的胜利。

Work context reveals whether outcome clarity is genuinely the problem. Teams drowning in hidden support work don’t need better goal setting; they need workload visibility and protection. Teams with clear outcomes but broken processes need operational fixes, not strategic realignment.

工作情境会揭示“结果不清晰”到底是不是真正的问题。被隐性支持工作淹没的团队，不需要更好的目标设定；他们需要的是工作量可见和被保护。那些结果清晰、但流程坏掉的团队，需要的是运营层面的修复，而不是战略层面的重新对齐。

Finally, the cultural context shapes what outcomes are politically viable. Some organizations reward visible feature delivery over infrastructure investment, but others punish anything that looks like it’s moving too fast. You need to work within these constraints while gradually shifting them.

最后，文化情境决定了哪些结果在政治上可行。有些组织奖励可见的功能交付、轻视基础设施投资；另一些则惩罚任何看起来“冲太快”的东西。你需要在这些约束之内工作，同时逐步地改变它们。

Failure Modes of Outcome Obsession

“结果执念”的失败模式

Outcome focus can become counterproductive when taken to extremes. This section outlines some of the warning signs to look out for that signify you’ve crossed the line.

聚焦结果一旦走向极端，就会适得其反。本节列出一些预警信号，提醒你已经过了那条线。

Measurement illusion

度量幻觉

This could include spending more time on tracking progress than making it, creating elaborate dashboards that nobody uses for decision making, or optimizing for metrics that don’t actually correlate with value.

这可能表现为：花在“追踪进展”上的时间比“取得进展”还多；做一堆没人用来做决策的华丽仪表盘；或者去优化那些其实和价值并不相关的指标。

— 原书第 69 页 —

We’ll talk more about metrics in Chapter 10.

关于指标，我们会在第 10 章详谈。

[插图：O’Reilly 装饰性动物图案]

Outcome rigidity

结果僵化

This includes refusing to adapt when you discover better approaches or when context changes, or treating initial outcome statements as unchangeable contracts rather than working hypotheses.

这包括：当你发现了更好的做法、或情境已经改变时却拒绝调整；或者把最初的结果表述当成不可更改的合同，而不是待检验的工作假设。

False precision

虚假精确

This refers to pretending that you can measure things that are genuinely unmeasurable, like team morale or code quality, rather than using qualitative assessment and human judgment.

这指的是：假装你能度量那些真正不可度量的东西——比如团队士气或代码质量——而不愿用定性评估和人的判断。

Gaming

博弈指标

In these cases, teams are optimizing for metrics rather than the underlying value and improving deployment frequency by breaking large changes into smaller, meaningless commits—hitting feature delivery targets by cutting quality or maintainability.

这种情况下，团队优化的是指标本身，而不是背后的价值：把大改动拆成一堆更小、毫无意义的 commit 来“提升”部署频率；靠牺牲质量或可维护性来达成功能交付目标。

The goal is outcome awareness, not outcome obsession. You want clarity on what matters without sacrificing the flexibility to adapt as you learn more.

目标是“结果觉察”，而不是“结果执念”。你希望对什么重要保持清晰，同时又不牺牲“随着认知加深而调整”的灵活性。

What This Looks Like in Practice

这在实践中长什么样

Consider a product team that is building a new feature. Instead of measuring completion percentage, you can track early user engagement signals. When engagement is lower than expected, you can pivot the approach rather than pushing toward the original deadline.

设想一个产品团队在做新功能。你不必度量“完成百分比”，而可以追踪早期的用户参与信号。当参与度低于预期时，你可以调转方向，而不是硬朝原定 deadline 冲。

As another example, an infrastructure team might be migrating to a new deployment system. Instead of measuring migration percentage, you can track time from code to production and assess the rollback success rate. When the new system performs worse than the old one, you can pause to fix core issues rather than continuing the migration.

再举一例：一个基础设施团队可能正在迁移到新的部署系统。你不必度量“迁移百分比”，而可以追踪“从代码到生产的时间”，并评估回滚成功率。当新系统表现不如旧系统时，你可以停下来修核心问题，而不是硬着头皮继续迁移。

Now consider a platform team that is building internal developer tools. Instead of measuring adoption rates, you can track developer productivity signals like time to onboard new team members or frequency of deployment pipeline failures. When productivity doesn’t improve, you can investigate workflow bottlenecks rather than adding more features.

再设想一个在做内部开发者工具的平台团队。你不必度量“采用率”，而可以追踪开发者生产率信号——比如新成员上手时间、部署流水线失败频率。当生产率没有提升时，你可以去排查工作流瓶颈，而不是再加更多功能。

— 原书第 70 页 —

Each example shows the same pattern: define outcomes that connect to larger value, measure leading indicators rather than lagging ones, and maintain a willingness to adapt when reality conflicts with the plan.

每个例子都是同一个模式：定义与更大价值相连的结果；度量先行指标而非滞后指标；并在现实与计划冲突时，保持调整的意愿。

Making It Sustainable

让它可持续

Outcome focus requires organizational discipline, not just individual discipline. You need systems that reinforce good decision making rather than hoping people will remember to think about impact. This includes:

聚焦结果需要组织层面的纪律，而不只是个人层面的纪律。你需要有系统来强化好的决策，而不是指望人们“记得”去想想影响。这包括：

  • Regular outcome reviews that ask “What did we achieve?” rather than “What did we ship?”

    定期的结果复盘，问的是“我们取得了什么？”而不是“我们发了什么？”

  • Team retrospectives that examine whether completed work actually solved problems

    团队复盘要检视：已完成的工作是否真的解决了问题

  • Planning sessions that start with desired outcomes rather than available work

    规划会从“想要的结果”出发，而不是从“手头现有的活”出发

The goal isn’t perfection but direction. You want teams that can answer “Why does this matter?” for the work they’re doing and “How will we know it worked?” for the changes they’re making.

目标不是完美，而是方向。你希望团队能对自己正在做的活回答“这件事为什么重要？”，也能对自己正在做的改变回答“我们怎么知道它奏效了？”

When outcome focus becomes habitual rather than forced, teams waste less energy on work that doesn’t matter and invest more energy in work that does. That’s the difference between being busy and being effective.

当聚焦结果从“刻意为之”变成“习惯成自然”时，团队浪费在无关工作上的精力会更少，投入在真正重要工作上的精力会更多。这就是“忙碌”与“有效”的区别。

Shift Between Roles

在角色间切换

Different moments call for different leadership styles.

不同的时刻，需要不同的领导风格。

Most leaders fail not from lack of skill but from rigid application of what worked before. They’ve mastered one approach—coaching, directing, or consensus building—and apply it regardless of context. That approach works well in stable environments where situations repeat predictably. However, in chaos, it’s a liability.

大多数领导者失败，不是因为缺技能，而是因为僵化地套用“过去管用的那一套”。他们精通某一种方式——教练式、指挥式、或共识式——然后不分情境地到处用。在局面可预测地重复的稳定环境里，这种方式很好使；但在混乱中，它就是负债。

The hardcore punk scene understood this intuitively. Different moments demanded different energy and approaches. Sometimes you needed strategic thinking to see the bigger picture. Sometimes you needed to tend to people who were struggling. Sometimes you had to get your hands dirty and do the work yourself.

硬核朋克圈子凭直觉就懂这一点。不同的时刻需要不同的能量和做法。有时你需要战略性思考去看见更大的图景；有时你需要去关照那些正在挣扎的人；有时你得亲自动手、卷起袖子自己干。

The effective leaders could read the room and adjust accordingly, expanding their range so they could meet the moment with what it actually needed.

有效的领导者能读懂现场、并据此调整，扩展自己的幅度，好用当下真正需要的东西去回应它。

The Cost of Leadership Rigidity

领导僵化的代价

Engineering leaders get trapped in familiar patterns for understandable reasons: a vice president who has built credibility through technical depth continues to delve into implementation details; a director who has earned trust through careful consensus building continues to facilitate when decisions need to be made quickly; a staff engineer who influences through expertise struggles to step back when the team needs space to learn.

工程领导者陷入熟悉模式，原因是可以理解的：一位靠技术深度建立公信力的 VP，会继续扎进实现细节里；一位靠谨慎建立共识赢得信任的总监，在需要快速决策时却还在继续主持讨论；一位靠专业施加影响的 staff 工程师，在团队需要空间去学习时，却很难退后半步。

— 原书第 71 页 —

These aren’t character flaws; they’re successful patterns that become limitations when overused. When the leader doesn’t recognize when the context has shifted, their default approach might no longer serve the situation.

这些不是性格缺陷；它们都是曾经成功过的模式，只是被过度使用后变成了局限。当领导者意识不到情境已经改变时，他们默认的那套做法可能已经不再适用于当下局面。

The problem deepens when your identity becomes fused with your style. “I’m a service-oriented leader” or “I lead through vision” stops being a description and becomes a constraint. You start defending your approach rather than questioning whether it fits the moment.

当你的身份和你的风格焊死在一起时，问题就更深了。“我是一个服务型领导者”或“我靠愿景领导”，不再是一句描述，而变成了一种束缚。你开始为自己的做法辩护，而不是去质疑它是否契合当下。

But leadership isn’t a personality trait or a brand you maintain—it’s a situational skill that adapts to what the team needs right now.

但领导力不是一种人格特质，也不是一个你要维护的品牌——它是一种情境化的技能，随团队此刻的需要而调整。

Three Essential Modes

三种核心模式

You don’t need to excel at every leadership style, but you need the ability to consciously shift between a few key modes based on what the situation demands. The three roles discussed in this section cover most of the territory you’ll face in chaotic environments.

你不需要精通每一种领导风格，但你需要有能力根据局面要求，在几种关键模式之间有意识地切换。本节讨论的三种角色，基本覆盖了你在混乱环境里会遇到的大部分场景。

The pilot: Zooming out for direction

领航员：拉远视角，看清方向

Being the pilot means holding a broader view. These leaders connect work to purpose, surface competing priorities, and help teams navigate when the path isn’t clear. This isn’t about having all the answers or being the smartest person in the room, but about creating clarity when everyone else is stuck in the details. You zoom out to see patterns, dependencies, and trade-offs that aren’t visible at ground level.

做领航员，意味着握着更宽的视野。这样的领导者把工作连回目的，把互相竞争的优先级摆上台面，并在路径不清时帮团队导航。这不是说你要拥有所有答案、或做屋里最聪明的人；而是当其他人都陷在细节里时，由你来创造清晰。你拉远视角，去看见那些在地面上看不见的模式、依赖关系和取舍。

Use pilot mode when priorities are unclear, teams are stuck in tactical debates, or you need to make sense of competing pressures from different stakeholders.

当优先级不清、团队陷在战术争论里、或你需要从不同利益相关方互相冲突的压力中理出头绪时，使用领航员模式。

This could look like:

它可能是这样的：

  • Stepping into a circular architecture discussion and reframing around user impact

    介入一场绕圈子的架构讨论，把焦点重新框定到用户影响上

  • Helping a team see how their technical decisions connect to business objectives

    帮团队看清他们的技术决策如何连回业务目标

  • Surfacing the real trade-offs when everyone’s talking past each other

    当大家各说各话时，把真正的取舍摆到台面上

— 原书第 72 页 —

When it backfires. Vision-setting can feel disconnected if the team is overwhelmed by immediate operational problems. Additionally, some cultures resist top-down direction, even when it’s collaborative. Your credibility for strategic thinking may depend on your background and position in the organization.

何时会适得其反。如果团队正被眼前的运营问题压得喘不过气，“定愿景”会显得脱离实际。此外，有些文化会抵触自上而下的指令，哪怕它是协作式的。你做战略思考的公信力，可能取决于你的背景和你在组织中的位置。

The medic: Stabilizing and rebuilding trust

医护：稳住局面，重建信任

The medic role focuses on people and relationships. They listen without agenda, help process difficult situations, and create space for recovery when things have been intense.

医护角色聚焦于人和关系。他们不带目的地倾听，帮人们消化艰难处境，并在局势紧张之后为恢复留出空间。

Rather than being a type of therapy or performance management, it involves recognizing when emotional dynamics are blocking progress and addressing them directly, instead of hoping they’ll resolve on their own.

它不是某种心理治疗，也不是绩效管理，而是：识别出情绪动态正在阻碍进展，并直接去处理它——而不是指望它自己消失。

Use medic mode when tension is rising, someone’s burned out or isolated, or when a difficult decision has landed and people need space to process.

当张力在上升、有人 burnout 或被孤立、或者一个艰难决定刚刚落地、人们需要空间去消化时，使用医护模式。

This could look like:

它可能是这样的：

  • Pulling aside a senior engineer who’s been unusually quiet and discovering they’re overwhelmed by scope changes

    把一位异常沉默的高级工程师拉到一边，发现他被范围变更压得喘不过气

  • Facilitating a conversation between team members who’ve been talking past each other

    在两位各说各话的团队成员之间，引导一场对话

  • Acknowledging that a reorganization was disruptive rather than pretending everyone should just adapt

    承认一次组织调整确实造成了冲击，而不是假装大家都该自动适应

When it backfires. Emotional labor can become an expectation rather than a choice, especially for leaders from underrepresented backgrounds. In addition, some organizational cultures punish leaders who spend time on “soft” issues. Your capacity for this work has limits that need protection.

何时会适得其反。情绪劳动可能从“一种选择”变成“一种理所当然的期待”——对来自代表性不足背景的领导者尤其如此。此外，有些组织文化会惩罚那些花时间在“软”问题上的领导者。你做这种工作的容量是有限的，需要被保护。

The engineer: Getting into the work

工程师：下场干活

The engineer role moves from observation to participation. They pair on difficult problems, debug blocked processes, and contribute directly rather than just directing from above.

工程师角色从观察转向参与。他们和人结对啃难题、排查卡住的流程、直接贡献代码，而不是只在上面发号施令。

Instead of being considered micromanagement, think of engineering mode as recognizing when the team needs you to roll up your sleeves and work alongside them, especially when technical complexity or organizational friction is creating barriers.

别把它当成微观管理；把“工程师模式”理解为：识别出团队什么时候需要你卷起袖子和他们并肩作战——尤其是当技术复杂度或组织摩擦正在制造障碍时。

Use engineer mode when momentum has stalled despite clarity, when critical details are blocking progress, or when the team needs to see that leadership is with them, not just watching from above.

当方向已经清晰、势头却依然停滞；当关键细节卡住了进展；或者当团队需要看到领导是和他们在一起、而不只是在上面看着时，使用工程师模式。

— 原书第 73 页 —

This could look like:

它可能是这样的：

  • Pairing with a junior developer on a complex migration

    和一位初级开发者结对，一起啃一个复杂的迁移

  • Sitting in on customer calls to understand requirements that keep changing

    旁听客户电话，去理解那些一直在变的需求

  • Writing the first draft of a process document rather than asking someone else to figure it out

    自己先写流程文档的第一稿，而不是丢给别人去想

When it backfires. Hands-on involvement can undermine team autonomy if overused. In addition, your technical skills may be outdated compared to those of your team, and getting pulled into implementation can distract from strategic responsibilities that only you can handle.

何时会适得其反。亲力亲为如果过度使用，会侵蚀团队的自主权。此外，你的技术能力可能已经落后于团队；而一旦被拉进实现细节，你就会从“只有你能处理的战略职责”上分走注意力。

The Switching Skill

切换这项技能

The real capability isn’t mastering any single mode but developing the judgment to switch consciously rather than subconsciously. This requires several key abilities.

真正的能力，不是精通某一种模式，而是练出那种“有意识地切换、而不是下意识地切换”的判断力。这需要几种关键能力。

Pattern recognition

模式识别

Certain signals will tell you that the current approach isn’t working: teams talking past each other, energy dropping in meetings, work stalling despite apparent activity, and learning to read these signals quickly and accurately.

某些信号会告诉你当前做法失效了：团队各说各话、会议里能量下降、看似忙碌工作却停滞不前。关键是学会快速而准确地读懂这些信号。

Mode flexibility

模式灵活

Can you shift approaches without losing authenticity? Some roles will feel more natural than others based on your background and strengths, but effectiveness matters more than comfort.

你能不能在不失去真实感的前提下切换做法？基于你的背景和优势，有些角色会比另一些更顺手；但有效，比舒服更重要。

Switching costs awareness

切换成本意识

Frequent role changes can confuse teams who need some predictability in leadership approach. The goal is conscious adaptation, not constant shifting. Teams need to understand why you’re changing approaches, not just experience the change.

频繁的角色切换会让团队困惑——他们需要领导方式有一定可预测性。目标是有意识的调适，而不是不停地变来变去。团队需要理解你为什么要改变做法，而不只是被动地经历这种改变。

The Reality of Constraints

约束的现实

It’s important to be aware that your ability to switch roles is limited. Identity, organizational position, and cultural context all affect which modes are available to you and how they’re received.

要清楚：你切换角色的能力是有限的。身份、组织位置、文化情境，都会影响你能用哪些模式、以及这些模式会被如何接收。

The goal isn’t to be everything to everyone, but to expand your effective range within your actual context and constraints.

目标不是对所有人都扮演一切角色，而是在你真实的情境和约束之内，扩展你有效的幅度。

— 原书第 74 页 —

Leading Through Others

通过他人去领导

As you move into more senior roles, your mode switching becomes more complex. You’re not just choosing your own approach but coordinating with other leaders and modeling flexibility for your team.

当你走向更高级的岗位，你的模式切换会变得更复杂。你不只是在选自己的做法，还要和其他领导协同，并为你的团队示范什么叫灵活。

This means helping your direct reports develop their own range rather than expecting them to mirror your style. A director who can shift between pilot and medic modes might work with managers who each have different strengths, creating collective range rather than individual completeness.

这意味着帮你的直接下属发展出他们自己的幅度，而不是指望他们照抄你的风格。一位能在领航员和医护模式间切换的总监，可能带着几位各有所长的经理一起工作，从而打造出“集体幅度”，而不是“个人全能”。

It also means reading the broader organizational context and helping your team understand when to match the moment versus when to maintain consistency. Sometimes the business needs everyone aligned on execution, and sometimes it needs different teams operating in different modes simultaneously.

这也意味着读懂更大的组织情境，并帮团队理解：什么时候该随当下调整、什么时候又该保持一致。有时候业务需要所有人在执行上对齐；有时候则需要不同团队同时运行在不同模式里。

The skill is knowing when your switch should be visible to the team and when it should be invisible. Sometimes you want people to understand why you’re changing approaches. Sometimes you just want them to experience the right leadership for the moment.

本事在于知道：你的切换什么时候该让团队看见、什么时候该隐于无形。有时候你希望人们理解你为什么要换做法；有时候你只是希望他们直接体验到“当下正好需要的那种领导”。

What This Looks Like in Practice

这在实践中长什么样

Consider the following examples of what this looks like in practice:

下面是几个实践中的例子：

  • Pilot mode. Your team is debating technical architecture but losing sight of user impact. You shift into pilot mode, step back from the technical details, and help them connect their decisions to customer outcomes.

    领航员模式。你的团队在争论技术架构，却渐渐忘了用户影响。你切到领航员模式，从技术细节里退出来，帮他们把决策连回客户结果。

  • Medic mode. A senior engineer has been unusually withdrawn since the last reorganization. You shift into medic mode, create space for a private conversation, and discover they’re questioning whether their expertise is still valued.

    医护模式。一位高级工程师自上次组织调整后异常退缩。你切到医护模式，留出一对一谈话的空间，发现他在怀疑自己的专业是否还被看重。

  • Engineer mode. A critical migration is stalled because of complex integration challenges. You shift into engineer mode, sit with the team, and work through the technical details until the path forward becomes clear.

    工程师模式。一次关键迁移因复杂的集成挑战而停滞。你切到工程师模式，和团队坐在一起，逐个啃技术细节，直到前路变得清晰。

The switching happens in response to what the team needs, not what feels comfortable or familiar. Over time, mode switching becomes habitual rather than forced, and your team learns to expect adaptability rather than rigid consistency.

这种切换是对“团队需要什么”做出的回应，而不是对“什么让你舒服或熟悉”的回应。久而久之，模式切换从刻意变成习惯，你的团队也开始期待“灵活适应”，而不是僵化的一致。

That’s the evolution from good technical leadership to effective organizational leadership, where you meet the needs of others rather than providing what you prefer.

这就是从“好的技术领导”到“有效的组织领导”的进化：你去满足他人的需要，而不是只提供你自己偏好的东西。

— 原书第 75 页 —

In Practice: April’s Story

实战案例：April 的故事

April walked into the post-incident meeting and immediately read the room. The business team wanted answers and timelines. Her senior engineers looked defensive and frustrated. The junior engineers were quiet, probably blaming themselves. April realized that the three different situations would require different approaches within the same meeting.

April 走进事故复盘会，立刻读懂了现场。业务团队要的是答案和时间表；她的高级工程师们看起来戒备又沮丧；初级工程师们很安静，大概在自责。April 意识到：在同一场会里，这三种不同处境需要不同的打法。

She started in pilot mode, connecting the outage to broader infrastructure needs and business impact. When she saw tension building between her team and product leadership, she switched to medic mode, acknowledging the stress everyone felt and creating space for honest conversation about capacity constraints. Finally, when the discussion stalled on technical details, she shifted to engineer mode, diving into the deployment process with her team to map out specific fixes. By the end of the meeting, they had achieved alignment on both immediate fixes and longer-term platform investment, moving beyond blame and defensiveness.

她先以领航员模式开场，把这次宕机连回更大的基础设施需求和业务影响。当她看到团队与产品领导层之间的张力上升时，切到医护模式，承认大家承受的压力，并留出空间坦诚讨论产能约束。最后，当讨论卡在技术细节上时，她切到工程师模式，和团队一起扎进部署流程，梳理出具体的修复方案。会议结束时，他们既对齐了眼下的修复，也对齐了长期的平台投资，走出了互相指责和戒备的状态。

Exercise: Practice Your Switches

练习：操练你的开关

This chapter is about developing range: the ability to read chaos and respond with what the situation actually needs. This exercise will help you to practice the four leadership switches using a real situation you’re facing.

本章讲的是发展幅度：读懂混乱、并用局面真正需要的东西去回应的能力。这个练习，会帮你用一个你正在面对的真实处境，来操练这四个领导开关。

Setup: Pick Your Chaos. Think of a current situation where standard leadership approaches aren’t working—something where you’ve tried the obvious solutions, but progress has stalled. Write it down in one sentence.

准备：选你的混乱。想一个眼下标准领导做法不管用的局面——一个你已经试过显而易见的解法、却依然停滞的局面。用一句话把它写下来。

Switch 1: Diagnose Context. Run your situation through the four lenses. Be honest; this only works if you see what’s actually happening:

开关 1：诊断情境。用四副透镜把你的处境过一遍。要诚实；只有你真的看见正在发生什么，这才管用。

  • System lens. Is this early-stage chaos (existential pressure), scale-up chaos (growth outpacing systems), or enterprise chaos (politics and interdependencies)?

    系统透镜。这是早期混乱（生存压力）、扩张期混乱（增长跑赢体系），还是企业期混乱（政治与相互依赖）？

  • Human lens. Are your people energized and ready for challenge, or exhausted and needing stability first? How’s the trust level?

    人的透镜。你的人是精力充沛、准备迎接挑战，还是已经耗竭、需要先稳住？信任水平如何？

— 原书第 76 页 —

  • Work lens. Is the real problem hidden work, unclear priorities, or unsustainable firefighting?

    工作透镜。真正的问题是隐性工作、不清的优先级，还是不可持续的救火？

  • Cultural lens. What leadership approaches get rewarded versus punished in your environment? What constraints do you actually face?

    文化透镜。在你的环境里，哪些领导方式被奖励、哪些被惩罚？你真正面对的约束是什么？

Write down the biggest insight from this diagnosis.

把这次诊断中最大的那条洞见写下来。

Switch 2: Thrive in Chaos. Based on your diagnosis, what does this moment need?

开关 2：在混乱中成长。基于你的诊断，当下这个时刻需要什么？

  • More momentum. What’s the smallest thing you could ship, fix, or decide this week to break the current pattern?

    更多势头。这周你能发出、修好或决定的最小一件事是什么？用它打破当前的模式。

  • More control. What structure would actually help people do their job (not just make you feel better)?

    更多控制。什么样的结构才是真能帮人们把活干成的（而不只是让你自己感觉好受）？

  • Different focus. What bureaucratic illusion could you eliminate to free up energy for real work?

    不同焦点。你能砍掉哪种“官僚幻觉”，好把精力解放出来投到真正的工作上？

Switch 3: Focus on Outcomes. What would actually happen if you solved this? Don’t write about “better communication” or “improved processes.” Write about the business or technical outcome that would make someone’s life genuinely better.

开关 3：聚焦结果。如果你把这个问题解决了，到底会发生什么？别写“更好的沟通”或“改进的流程”。要写那个能让某个人的日子真正变好的业务或技术结果。

Switch 4: Shift Between Roles. Given everything above, which role does this situation need right now?

开关 4：在角色间切换。综合以上一切，这个局面此刻需要哪个角色？

  • Pilot. Should you zoom out and help people see connections they’re missing?

    领航员。你该拉远视角，帮人们看见他们没看到的联系吗？

  • Medic. Does someone need space to process before you can move forward?

    医护。在你继续前进之前，是否有人需要空间去消化？

  • Engineer. Do you need to roll up your sleeves and work alongside the team?

    工程师。你需要卷起袖子和团队并肩作战吗？

Write down which mode you’ll try first and one specific action you’ll take in the next three days.

写下你会先试哪种模式，以及未来三天内你会采取的一个具体行动。

— 原书第 77 页 —

Exercise: Practice Your Switches (continued) — Reality Check

练习：操练你的开关（续）——现实检验

Reality Check. Look at what you wrote. Does it match what you’ve been doing, or does it suggest a different approach? If you’re not planning to change anything, run through the diagnosis again. You probably missed something important.

现实检验。看看你写下来的东西。它和你一直在做的事一致吗？还是指向一种不同的做法？如果你不打算改变任何事，那就把诊断再走一遍。你很可能漏掉了某个重要的东西。

The point isn’t to solve everything perfectly. It’s to practice reading chaos and choosing conscious responses instead of defaulting to what feels familiar.

重点不是把一切都完美解决。重点是练习读懂混乱、并选择有意识的回应，而不是退回到那些让人熟悉的默认反应。

Conclusion: Pulling It All Together

结语：把一切串起来

Engineering leadership rarely starts in calm waters. You inherit chaos in all its glory. You don’t get to wait for someone else to fix it. That’s the work.

工程领导很少从风平浪水中启程。你接手的是一团“精彩纷呈”的混乱。你没资格等别人来修好它——这就是你的活。

What we’ve learned from punk, hardcore, and open source is that you don’t beat chaos with control. You don’t earn trust with posturing. You don’t build momentum by waiting for the whole picture. Instead, you act, commit, and teach. Show up again and again, because that consistency is what turns noise into clarity.

我们从朋克、硬核和开源中学到的是：你不是用控制去战胜混乱的；你不是靠摆姿态赢得信任的；你也不是靠等“看清全貌”来建立势头的。相反，你行动、你承诺、你言传身教。一次又一次地到场——正是这种一致性，把噪音变成清晰。

The four switches we’ve covered aren’t separate tools; they work together. Context diagnosis helps you determine which moments require which approach. Thriving in chaos creates momentum that aligns with what you’ve read. Outcome focus keeps you pointed toward impact as you adapt. Role flexibility gives you the range to meet different situations with what they need.

我们讲的这四个开关，并不是几件孤立的工具；它们是协同工作的。情境诊断帮你判断哪些时刻需要哪种做法；在混乱中成长，制造出与你的读懂相匹配的势头；聚焦结果，让你在调整时始终指向影响；角色灵活，则给你幅度，用不同局面所需的东西去回应它们。

Not every approach survives and not every team makes it through. But the spirit and the ethos of building, adapting, and persisting outlasts the moment and creates something bigger than any individual effort.

并非每种做法都能存活，也并非每个团队都能熬过来。但那种“建设、调适、坚持”的精神与气质，会比这个时刻更长久，并创造出比任何个人努力都更大的东西。

This is how you turn chaos into productivity. This is how you lead when the map doesn’t match the territory and the rules keep changing. You read the context, focus on what matters, switch between what the team needs, identify the hard choices, and build systems that enable others to do the same.

这就是你把混乱变成产出的方式。这就是当地图和地形对不上、规则还一直在变时，你如何领导。你读懂情境、聚焦重要之事、在团队所需之间切换、识别出艰难的取舍，并搭建系统让其他人也能如法炮制。

Remember: range beats rigidity and motion creates clarity and persistence, with principles that outlast any single crisis. That’s leadership in chaos—and how you build something that lasts.

请记住：幅度胜过僵化，行动催生清晰与坚持，而原则会比任何一场危机都更长寿。这就是混乱中的领导力——也是你如何建造出某种持久之物的方式。

In Chapter 4, we’ll talk about building cohesive teams using some of these switches.

在第 4 章，我们会谈谈如何运用其中一些开关，去打造有凝聚力的团队。
